newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece hit by strikes, farmers' road blockade.
newsitem.headline: Greece hit by strikes, farmers' road blockade.

text.p: Greece faced a new wave of strikes to protest against the ruling socialists' tax-intensive economic policies on Tuesday and a farmers' road blockade crippled land transport for the 20th day.
Civil servants have called a one-day strike on Tuesday and the General Confederation of Greek Workers (GSEE) -- the biggest labour grouping -- has called a three-hour solidarity stoppage.
Both groups will rally outside the central Athens parliament in the evening when a five-day debate begins on the 1997 budget.
An array of unions -- from teachers, doctors and seamen to government bureaucrats and diplomats -- have called strikes and marches ahead of the vote on the budget on Saturday night.

Workers have demanded better pensions, higher minimum wages and expressed outrage at heavier taxation. The socialists have boosted indirect taxes on items such as alcohol and swept away hundreds of tax exemptions.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis, a taciturn pro-European economist, is locked in an increasingly bitter fight with the nation's farmers -- once the backbone of his socialist party.
He again rejected any concessions to the farmers' demands on Monday, saying the government had no more money to give.
"We cannot give away hundreds of billions of drachmas. We would lose our chances of development. We would lose our chances of socialist justice," he told reporters.
The farmers have posed the most serious threat to Simitis since he won elections in September, vowing to take the steps needed to push the economy into line with Greece's European Union partners.
Simitis, who has appeared rarely since the farmers' revolt began, looked agitated but determined not to give in, saying he wanted a solution with "no winners and no losers".
He rejected direct talks with the farmers until they lifted the blockades which have wreaked havoc on the economy and land transport for three weeks.
The farmers want lower fuel prices, higher price supports, lower Value Added Tax (VAT) on their equipment and rescheduling $1.3 billion in debts.

They have appeared increasingly divided in recent days over how to continue the blockades, and many barricades have been lifted, but a hard core still has the main north-south road cut, dividing the country in two.
Seamen began a two-day strike on Monday and commercial ships and ferries were at a standstill. They want their pension fund overhauled.
Their strike made circumventing the farmers' blockade more difficult and further tarnished Greece's reputation with tourists trying to take ferries to islands.

Many farmers' representatives in the central stronghold of Larissa reacted angrily to Simitis's latest refusal to meet them. They have threatened to descend on Athens on Wednesday during the budget debate.

"The government holds the key to breaking the deadlock. The government must meet us without pre-conditions. Otherwise we will block the roads through Christmas," said Larissa farmers' leader Yannis Pattakis.
